title: God, Creation, Signs and the Last Day
bigQuestion: What does the Qur'an say about God, the world and what comes after it, and how do Muslims read those passages?

story.title: Look at the Camel
story.kicker: A middle-school class reads four lines that point at four ordinary things and ask one question.
paragraphs: Ms. Ortiz writes four lines on the board. They come from Surah 88, called Al-Ghashiyah, The Overwhelming. She uses Pickthall's 1930 translation. "Will they not regard the camels, how they are created? And the heaven, how it is raised? And the hills, how they are set up? And the earth, how it is spread?" She reads them twice. Then she waits.

Dani puts a hand up. "Why a camel? That seems random." Ms. Ortiz smiles. "Who first heard these lines?" The class thinks. Someone says: people in Mecca, around the year 615. "And what did they see every day?" Camels. Sky. Mountains. Dry ground. The four things are not random. They are the whole world of a person in western Arabia.

The class notices something else. The lines do not say "a camel is a sign." They ask a question. "Will they not regard?" means "Will they not look?" The verse treats looking as a duty. Ms. Ortiz explains a word. The Arabic word for a verse of the Qur'an is ayah. It also means "a sign." So for Muslims, the Qur'an calls its own verses signs, and it calls the sky and the camel signs too.

"So the book and the world are both supposed to point at the same thing?" Dani asks. "That is how Muslim scholars have read it," Ms. Ortiz says. "They believe both point to one God. Our job in this class is different. We read the lines, we ask who heard them, and we ask what the lines are doing."

She turns back to the board. "These four lines are doing something. They are giving an argument, but without the word 'therefore.' Your task: write the missing 'therefore' in your own words. Then we will see what the surah says next."
story.think: The verse asks its hearers to look at four things they saw every day. Why might a text argue by pointing instead of by stating?

lessons.title: Tawhid in Four Lines
lessons.mainIdea: Tawhid, the belief that God is one and has no partner, is the center of the Qur'an, and Surah 112 states it in four short verses.
reading: Surah 112 is called Al-Ikhlas, Sincerity or Purity. It is one of the shortest surahs in the Qur'an. It has four verses. Muslims recite it in daily prayer, and many children learn it early. A hadith reported in the collection of Bukhari says Muhammad called it equal to one third of the Qur'an. Muslim scholars read that as praise of its subject, not its length.

The subject is *tawhid*. The word comes from an Arabic root that means "to make one." It names the belief that God is one, has no partner, no parent and no child, and that nothing is like God. Muslims consider tawhid the first and most important teaching of their faith. The surah says it in the plainest possible way. It does not tell a story or give a law. It states who God is and who God is not.

The surah opens with the command "Say." Many surahs do. Muslims read this as God telling Muhammad what to say to the people of Mecca. Those people, according to Muslim tradition, honored many gods and kept idols at the Kaaba. Some also spoke of daughters of God. Read in that setting, each line of the surah answers a claim its first hearers had heard. Historians note that we know the Meccan setting mainly from Muslim sources written later.

The surah also speaks to Christians and Jews, according to many commentators. Al-Tabari, who wrote in the 900s, records reports that people asked Muhammad to describe his God, and this surah came as the answer. The phrase "He begetteth not nor was begotten" is read by Muslim scholars as denying that God has a son. Christians read their own scripture differently. The course describes both readings without deciding between them.

words.d: the Muslim belief that God is one, with no partner, parent or child
Surah 112, a four-verse surah that states tawhid; its name means Sincerity or Purity
a reported saying or action of Muhammad, collected and graded by later scholars

look.title: Surah 112 in Pickthall's Translation
look.text: Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him.
look.cite: Qur'an 112:1–4 (Al-Ikhlas), Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Each of the four lines says something God is or is not. List the four claims in your own words. Which one answers the idea of "daughters of God" that Muslim tradition says Meccans held?

check.q: What does the word tawhid mean in Islam?
choices: The belief that God is one and has no partner
The rule of fasting during Ramadan
The order of surahs in the Qur'an
The blessing said after Muhammad's name
check.why: Tawhid comes from a root meaning "to make one" and names the belief in one God with no partner.

check.q: Surah 112 begins with the word "Say." How do Muslims read that opening?
choices: As God telling Muhammad what to say to people
As a note added by later copyists
As the title of the surah
check.why: Muslims read "Say" as God addressing Muhammad, who then delivers the words to his hearers.

check.q: Why do Muslim scholars say a hadith calls Al-Ikhlas equal to a third of the Qur'an?
choices: Because it is a third of the book's length
Because it was revealed in three parts
Because its subject, tawhid, is central to the whole book
Because it is recited three times a day
check.why: Scholars read the hadith as praise of the surah's subject, tawhid, which they consider the Qur'an's central teaching.

lessons.title: The Ninety-Nine Names
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims describe God through names found in the Qur'an, traditionally counted as ninety-nine, and the names of mercy come first and most often.
reading: The Qur'an does not describe God's shape or face. It describes God by names. Verse 7:180 says that the most beautiful names belong to God and tells believers to call on God by them. A hadith in the collections of Bukhari and Muslim says God has ninety-nine names. From that report, Muslim scholars built lists. The lists differ a little from one scholar to another, and the Qur'an itself uses more than ninety-nine.

Two names come first. Every surah but one opens with the *basmala*: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful." That is Pickthall's wording. The two Arabic words are ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim. Both come from a root that means mercy or a mother's womb. Muslim commentators such as Ibn Kathir explain that ar-Rahman names mercy as God's nature, while ar-Rahim names mercy in action toward creatures.

Other names appear again and again. Al-'Alim, the Knower. Al-Hakim, the Wise. Al-'Adl, the Just. Al-Ghafur, the Forgiving. Al-Khaliq, the Creator. Al-Malik, the King. Muslims often recite the names on a string of beads called a misbaha. Many Muslim children are named after the names, with the word 'abd, "servant of," in front: Abdullah, Abd ar-Rahman, Abd al-Karim.

Scholars in the tradition read the names as pairs that balance. God is described as the Just and the Forgiving, the One who lowers and the One who raises, the First and the Last. The Sufi tradition, the mystical side of Islam, uses the names in long repeated prayer called dhikr, "remembrance." Sunni and Shia Muslims share the names, though some of their lists and prayers differ.

words.d: the phrase "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful" that opens every surah except Surah 9
one of the two names of mercy in the basmala, often translated the Beneficent or the Most Gracious
"remembrance"; repeating God's names or short phrases as a prayer, especially in Sufi practice

look.title: Two Words for Mercy
look.text: Pickthall (1930) translates the basmala: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful." Rodwell (1861) translates it: "In the Name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful." Sale (1734) has: "In the name of the most merciful God." The Arabic has two different words from one root, ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim.
look.prompt: Which translator keeps two separate words for the two Arabic names, and which one folds them into one? What is gained or lost in each choice?

check.q: Where do Muslims say the number ninety-nine for God's names comes from?
choices: From the number of surahs in the first juz'
From a count of names in the Torah
From the age of Muhammad at his death
From a hadith reported in Bukhari and Muslim
check.why: A hadith in the collections of Bukhari and Muslim says God has ninety-nine names; scholars built their lists from it.

check.q: Which two names open almost every surah in the basmala?
choices: Ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim, the two names of mercy
check.why: The basmala reads "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful," using ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim.

check.q: What is dhikr?
choices: The list of a surah's verses
Repeating God's names or short phrases as a prayer
The call to prayer from a mosque
check.why: Dhikr means "remembrance" and names the practice of repeating God's names, common among Sufis and other Muslims.

lessons.title: The Throne Verse
lessons.mainIdea: Ayat al-Kursi, the Throne Verse (2:255), gathers the Qur'an's picture of God into one verse that Muslims memorize and recite for protection.
reading: In the middle of the longest surah sits the verse many Muslims call the greatest in the Qur'an. It is 2:255, in Surah Al-Baqarah, The Cow. Its name is Ayat al-Kursi, the Throne Verse, from the word kursi, "throne" or "footstool," near its end. A hadith in Muslim's collection reports Muhammad naming it the greatest verse. Many Muslims recite it after each prayer and before sleep.

The verse is one long sentence in Arabic. It moves through a list. God is living and does not sleep. Everything in the heavens and earth belongs to God. No one can speak for another before God without permission. God knows the past and future of every person, and people know only what God allows. Then the throne, which the verse says holds the heavens and the earth. Then two final names: the Sublime, the Tremendous.

Muslim readers have argued about the word kursi. Some early commentators, quoted by al-Tabari, took it as God's knowledge. Others took it as a real throne or footstool beyond the heavens. Ibn Kathir reports both views. The school of thought called Ash'ari taught that such words are true but that their manner is unknown to us. The Mu'tazila, an early rationalist school, read them as pure symbols. These debates show that one verse can hold many careful readings inside one faith.

Historians of religion notice something else. The verse shares images with the Hebrew Bible, where Psalm 121 says the guardian of Israel does not slumber or sleep. Scholars discuss whether the Qur'an echoes that language on purpose. Muslims believe the Qur'an confirms earlier scripture, so a shared image is no surprise to them. Academic readers see it as evidence that the Qur'an spoke to hearers who knew biblical stories.

words.d: the Throne Verse, Qur'an 2:255, which many Muslims call the greatest verse in the book
Arabic for "throne" or "footstool"; the word that gives 2:255 its name
a major Sunni school of theology that accepts the Qur'an's descriptions of God without asking how they work

look.title: The Throne Verse, Opening and Close
look.text: Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him. Unto Him belongeth whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is in the earth. [...] His throne includeth the heavens and the earth, and He is never weary of preserving them. He is the Sublime, the Tremendous.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:255 (Al-Baqarah), Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930; middle clauses omitted
look.prompt: List every claim the verse makes about God. Which claims are about power, and which are about knowledge? Why might a reader recite this verse before sleeping?

check.q: Where is the Throne Verse found?
check.why: Ayat al-Kursi is 2:255, in the middle of Surah Al-Baqarah, the longest surah.

check.q: How did the Ash'ari school handle the word "throne" in 2:255?
choices: They removed the word from their copies
They accepted it as true but said its manner is unknown
They said it proved God has a body like ours
They said it referred to the Kaaba
check.why: Ash'ari theology accepts such descriptions as true without asking how they work, unlike the Mu'tazila, who read them as symbols.

check.q: Why does a shared image between Psalm 121 and the Throne Verse not surprise Muslim readers?
choices: Because Muslims believe the Qur'an confirms earlier scripture
Because the Psalms were written after the Qur'an
Because the two texts are in the same language
check.why: Muslims believe the Qur'an confirms the earlier books, so a shared image fits their view; academic readers discuss it as evidence of the audience's knowledge.

lessons.title: The Heavens and the Earth
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an describes God creating the heavens and the earth in six days, with no rest afterward, and describes creation as ongoing.
reading: The Qur'an speaks of creation in many places, but it never tells the story in one long passage as Genesis 1 does. It gives short pieces. Verse 7:54 says God created the heavens and the earth in six days and then took the throne. Verse 41:9–12 lists the earth, its mountains and food, then the sky, in stages. Verse 21:30 says the heavens and the earth were one piece, then were parted, and that every living thing was made from water.

Readers who know Genesis notice a difference right away. Genesis 2:2 says God rested on the seventh day. The Qur'an says in 50:38 that no weariness touched God. Muslim commentators such as Ibn Kathir point to this as a correction of an earlier idea. Jewish and Christian commentators read "rested" as "ceased" rather than as being tired. The two traditions read their own texts, and the difference is in the wording each one starts from.

The Qur'an also speaks of creation as still going on. Verse 55:29 says every day God is at work. Verse 35:1 says God adds to creation as God wills. Muslim theologians used these verses to argue that the world depends on God at every moment, not only at the start. In the Qur'an, a *khalq*, a "creation," is not only an event but a relationship.

Modern Muslim readers have asked how these verses fit with science. Some read "six days" as six long ages, since the Qur'an says in 22:47 that a day with God is like a thousand years. Others say the verses teach who made the world, not how, and leave the how to science. Some Muslims reject parts of modern science. The course reports these views without ranking them.

words.d: Arabic for "creation," both the act of creating and what is created
the span of creation the Qur'an names in 7:54 and elsewhere, read by Muslims in different ways

look.title: Two Texts on the Seventh Day
look.text: Genesis 2:2 (King James Version, 1611): "And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made." Qur'an 50:38, in paraphrase: God created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no weariness touched God.
look.prompt: What does each text say happened after the six days? How does each tradition explain the word "rested" or its absence? What would a reader miss by reading only one text?

check.q: How does the Qur'an present the creation story compared with Genesis 1?
choices: In one long passage, day by day
In short pieces scattered across many surahs
Only as a list of animals
check.why: The Qur'an gives creation in short pieces (7:54, 41:9–12, 21:30) rather than one continuous account.

check.q: What does Qur'an 50:38 say that Muslim commentators contrast with Genesis 2:2?
choices: That the earth was made before the sky
That every living thing came from water
That no weariness touched God after creation
check.why: Ibn Kathir and others read 50:38's "no weariness" as correcting the idea that God rested from tiredness.

check.q: How do some modern Muslim readers explain "six days"?
choices: As six separate creations of six worlds
check.why: Some Muslims read "days" as ages, pointing to 22:47, where a day with God is like a thousand years.

lessons.title: Signs in Nature
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an calls things in nature ayat, signs, and asks its hearers to look at them as evidence of one Creator.
reading: The Arabic word *ayah* has two meanings in the Qur'an. It is a verse of the book. It is also a sign, a mark that points to something beyond itself. The Qur'an uses the second meaning hundreds of times. Rain, wind, ships on the sea, the change of night and day, the growth of crops, bees, cattle, the stars: each is named as a sign "for people who think" or "for people who reflect."

Surah 88:17–20, the lines in this chapter's opening story, are the most famous example. Surah 16, An-Nahl, The Bee, is another. It runs through cattle, rain, crops, the sea, mountains, rivers and stars, and then the bee, which the surah says was inspired to build its house and make a drink of many colors that heals. Surah 30:20–25 lists the making of humans from dust, the pairing of spouses, the variety of languages and skin colors, sleep, lightning and rain, each introduced by "among His signs."

The argument is always the same. The world is ordered, the order is a gift, and the gift points to a giver. Muslim theologians later turned this into a formal proof for God's existence. The Qur'an itself does not argue formally. It points. Al-Ghazali, a scholar who died in 1111, wrote that the ordinary person needs no proof beyond looking at the sky. Modern readers have called this the Qur'an's "argument from design."

This idea shaped Muslim science. Astronomers in Baghdad and Cairo, working in the 800s and after, wrote that studying the sky was a way to read God's signs. Some Muslim writers today say the same about biology. Others warn against making the Qur'an a science textbook, since the verses are meant to move the heart, not to give data. Both are Muslim readings of the same lines.

words.d: a verse of the Qur'an; also "a sign," anything in nature or history that points to God
Surah 16, The Bee, which lists many signs in nature and takes its name from the bee in verse 68
the idea that the order in the world points to a maker; modern readers use it for the Qur'an's sign verses

look.title: Four Questions in Surah 88
look.text: Will they not regard the camels, how they are created? And the heaven, how it is raised? And the hills, how they are set up? And the earth, how it is spread?
look.cite: Qur'an 88:17–20 (Al-Ghashiyah), Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Each line asks about how something came to be. Rewrite the four questions as one statement that begins "Because...". What does the verse expect its hearers to conclude?

check.q: What are the two meanings of ayah in the Qur'an?
check.why: Ayah means a verse of the book and also a sign, such as rain or the stars, that points to God.

check.q: Surah 16 is named for which sign in nature?
check.why: Surah 16, An-Nahl, takes its name from the bee, which verse 68 says was inspired to build its house.

check.q: What did al-Ghazali say about proving God's existence?
choices: That the ordinary person needs no proof beyond looking at the sky
That only the Throne Verse proves it
check.why: Al-Ghazali (d. 1111) wrote that looking at the sky was proof enough for ordinary people, echoing the Qur'an's sign verses.

lessons.title: Angels and Jinn
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an describes angels as God's messengers made of light and jinn as unseen beings made of fire who, like humans, can choose.
reading: The Qur'an speaks of beings that people cannot see. The first kind is angels, mala'ika in Arabic. Belief in angels is one of the six articles of faith that Sunni Muslims list, drawn from verses such as 2:285. The Qur'an names Jibril (Gabriel), who Muslims believe brought the revelation to Muhammad, and Mikail (Michael). Muslim tradition adds Israfil, who will blow the trumpet on the Last Day, and the angel of death.

Angels have jobs. Some carry the throne, according to 69:17. Two sit at each person's shoulders and write down deeds, according to 50:17–18 and 82:10–12. Some guard hell. Some bring rain. The Qur'an says angels do not disobey God, in 66:6. The hadith collections add that angels are made of light, though the Qur'an itself does not say so. Angels in the Qur'an have no gender, and 43:19 rebukes those who called them female.

The second kind is *jinn*. Surah 72 is named for them. The Qur'an says in 55:15 that jinn were made from smokeless fire, and in 51:56 that jinn and humans were both created to serve God. Unlike angels, jinn can choose. Some believe, some do not. Surah 72 describes a group of jinn who heard the Qur'an and accepted it. Muslim tradition says Iblis, the figure the Qur'an calls Shaytan (Satan), was a jinn who refused to bow to Adam, as told in 18:50.

Jinn passed into folk stories across the Muslim world, and from there into English as "genie." Muslim scholars separate the Qur'an's picture from those tales. Some modern Muslim thinkers read jinn as symbols for hidden forces; most Muslims take them as real beings. Historians note that pre-Islamic Arabs also spoke of jinn, so the Qur'an used a word its hearers already knew and gave it a new place in a story about one God.

words.d: Arabic for angels; in the Qur'an, God's servants and messengers who do not disobey
unseen beings the Qur'an says were made of smokeless fire, who can choose belief or unbelief
the figure Muslim tradition identifies as Shaytan (Satan), a jinn who refused to bow to Adam

look.title: Two Kinds of Unseen Beings
look.text: The Qur'an says angels do not disobey what God commands (66:6). It says of the jinn, in Surah 72, that some are righteous and some are otherwise, on different paths. It says Iblis was of the jinn and disobeyed (18:50).
look.prompt: Using only these three verses, explain the difference between an angel and a jinn in the Qur'an. Why does it matter to the story of Adam that Iblis was a jinn and not an angel?

check.q: According to the Qur'an, which angel do Muslims believe brought the revelation to Muhammad?
check.why: Muslims believe Jibril, Gabriel, brought the Qur'an to Muhammad; Mikail is also named, and Israfil comes from tradition.

check.q: What does the Qur'an say jinn were made from?
check.why: Qur'an 55:15 says jinn were made from smokeless fire; the hadith, not the Qur'an, say angels are made of light.

check.q: How do jinn differ from angels in the Qur'an's account?
choices: Jinn are visible and angels are not
Jinn can choose belief or unbelief; angels do not disobey
check.why: Surah 72 shows jinn on different paths, while 66:6 says angels do not disobey; Iblis, a jinn, chose to refuse.

lessons.title: One Message, Many Messengers
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an names about twenty-five prophets, most of them figures from the Bible, and says they all taught the same message of one God.
reading: Muslims believe God sent messengers to every people. The Qur'an says so in 10:47 and 16:36. It names about twenty-five *prophets*, though the exact count depends on how a reader treats a few names. Most of them appear in the Hebrew Bible or the New Testament: Adam, Nuh (Noah), Ibrahim (Abraham), Musa (Moses), Dawud (David), Sulayman (Solomon), Yunus (Jonah), Isa (Jesus). A few, such as Hud and Salih, are Arabian figures not found in the Bible.

The Qur'an mentions Musa (Moses) more than any other prophet, well over a hundred times. Ibrahim (Abraham) comes next. Muhammad is named only four times, plus once as Ahmad. Muslim scholars explain this pattern. The Qur'an is addressed to Muhammad, so it does not need to name him. It tells the stories of earlier prophets as lessons for him and his hearers, who were facing the same rejection those prophets faced.

Muslim tradition sorts messengers into two groups. A *nabi*, prophet, receives revelation. A *rasul*, messenger, also brings a book or a law. Every rasul is a nabi, but not every nabi is a rasul. Five are called "those of firm resolve" in 46:35, usually named as Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad. Muslims believe Muhammad is the last of them, the "seal of the prophets," a phrase from 33:40.

The Qur'an says in 2:136 that Muslims make no distinction among the messengers, meaning that they accept all of them. Jewish and Christian readers hold different views of some of these figures. Jews do not count Jesus or Muhammad as prophets. Christians hold beliefs about Jesus that the Qur'an does not share. Each tradition reads the shared figures through its own book. This course describes those readings side by side.

words.d: a person Muslims believe God chose to receive and deliver a message; nabi in Arabic
a prophet, one who receives revelation; the broader of the Qur'an's two terms
a messenger, a prophet who also brings a book or law; every rasul is also a nabi
a phrase from Qur'an 33:40 that Muslims read to mean Muhammad is the last prophet

look.title: How Often Some Prophets Are Named
look.cite: Commonly cited concordance counts of the Arabic text; scholars' totals differ slightly by counting method
look.prompt: Muhammad is named far less than Musa. What reason do Muslim scholars give? What does the list suggest about the stories the Qur'an's first hearers already knew?

check.q: Which prophet does the Qur'an mention most often?
check.why: Musa (Moses) is named well over a hundred times, more than any other prophet; Muhammad is named only four times.

check.q: What is the difference between a nabi and a rasul in Muslim tradition?
choices: A nabi is a prophet; a rasul also brings a book or law
A nabi is a Jewish prophet; a rasul is Arabian
A nabi is female; a rasul is male
A nabi is a scribe; a rasul is a reciter
check.why: Every rasul, messenger, is a nabi, prophet, but a rasul also brings a book or a law, such as Musa with the Torah.

check.q: What does "seal of the prophets" in 33:40 mean to Muslims?
check.why: Muslims read 33:40 to mean that Muhammad closes the line of prophets, so no prophet comes after him.

lessons.title: Torah, Psalms, Gospel, Qur'an
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an names earlier scriptures, the Torah, the Psalms and the Gospel, and says it confirms them while Muslims believe it also corrects and completes them.
reading: The Qur'an names four books that Muslims believe God sent. The *Tawrat*, the Torah, given to Musa (Moses). The *Zabur*, the Psalms, given to Dawud (David). The *Injil*, the Gospel, given to Isa (Jesus). And the Qur'an itself, given to Muhammad. Verse 3:3 names the first three together and says the Qur'an confirms them. Verse 5:44 calls the Torah guidance and light. Verse 5:46 says the same of the Gospel.

Because of these books, the Qur'an gives Jews and Christians a special name: *People of the Book*, Ahl al-Kitab. The phrase appears more than thirty times. Some verses address them warmly, such as 29:46, which tells Muslims to argue with them only in the kindest way and to say "our God and your God is one." Other verses criticize them, and the Qur'an also accuses some of altering or hiding their scripture, in 2:75 and 3:78.

Muslim scholars debate what that accusation means. Some, such as Ibn Hazm in the 1000s, held that the text itself was changed. Others, including many modern scholars, held that the words are sound and only the reading was twisted. Jewish and Christian scholars hold that their scriptures were handed down faithfully. This is a real disagreement, and the course names it rather than settling it.

One more point matters for reading. The Qur'an uses "Injil," Gospel, in the singular, as one book given to Isa. Christians have four Gospels, written by four authors about Jesus. Muslims generally believe the original Injil was a single revelation, now lost or changed. Christian readers see the four Gospels as the Gospel. Knowing this difference explains a good deal of what each side says about the other's book.

words.d: the Torah, the book the Qur'an says was given to Musa (Moses)
the Psalms, the book the Qur'an says was given to Dawud (David)
the Gospel, the book the Qur'an says was given to Isa (Jesus), named in the singular
Ahl al-Kitab, the Qur'an's name for Jews and Christians, who received earlier scriptures

look.title: Earlier Books Named in the Qur'an
look.cite: Commonly cited concordance counts of the Arabic text; totals differ slightly by counting method
look.prompt: Which earlier book does the Qur'an name most? Given that Musa is also the prophet named most, what might that say about who the Qur'an's first hearers were talking with?

check.q: Which book does the Qur'an say was given to Dawud (David)?
check.why: The Zabur, the Psalms, is the book the Qur'an connects to Dawud; the Tawrat goes with Musa and the Injil with Isa.

check.q: Who does the Qur'an mean by the People of the Book?
choices: Jews and Christians, who received earlier scriptures
The scribes who wrote the Qur'an
check.why: Ahl al-Kitab names Jews and Christians, whose scriptures the Qur'an recognizes as sent from God.

check.q: How do most Muslims understand the word "Injil" differently from Christians?
choices: Muslims say it means the Psalms
Muslims say it was given to Musa
Muslims mean one book given to Isa; Christians have four Gospels about Jesus
Muslims say it was written in Arabic
check.why: The Qur'an uses Injil in the singular for a revelation to Isa, while Christians read four Gospels as the Gospel.

lessons.title: Judgment and the Scales
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an describes a Day of Judgment when the dead rise, deeds are weighed, and each person answers for what they did.
reading: After tawhid, no theme fills the Meccan surahs more than the Last Day. The Qur'an gives it many names: the Day of Judgment, the Day of Resurrection, the Hour, the Overwhelming, the Calamity. Surah 81 describes the sun folded up, the stars falling and the seas boiling. Surah 99, Az-Zalzalah, The Earthquake, describes the earth shaking out its burdens and telling its news.

On that day, according to the Qur'an, every person is raised. Each receives a record. Verse 17:13–14 says the book is opened and the person is told to read it. Verse 21:47 says scales are set up, and no one is wronged by even a mustard seed's weight. Verse 99:7–8 says whoever did an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever did an atom's weight of evil will see it. The picture is of complete fairness.

Muslim readers of Mecca's first hearers note why the theme mattered. Muslim tradition says many Meccans laughed at the idea of bones rising, and 36:78–79 records that mockery and answers it. The theme also carried a moral edge. If every deed is weighed, then the rich who ignored the orphan and cheated in trade would answer for it. Many of the earliest surahs join the Last Day to justice for the poor.

Muslims across all schools believe in the Day of Judgment; it is one of the six articles of faith. They differ on details. Some read the scales as literal; some read them as a figure for perfect justice. Shia and Sunni traditions both hold that Muhammad will intercede for believers on that day, drawing on hadith, though the Qur'an in 2:255 says no one intercedes without God's permission. The theme of judgment appears in Jewish and Christian texts too, and scholars compare the pictures.

words.d: Yawm ad-Din, the day the Qur'an says the dead will rise and every deed will be judged
the mizan, the balance the Qur'an says will weigh each person's deeds on the Last Day
pleading on another person's behalf; in Islam, Muhammad's plea for believers, which the Qur'an says needs God's permission

look.title: An Atom's Weight
look.text: Surah 99 ends by saying that on that day people will come forward in groups to be shown their deeds. Whoever has done an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever has done an atom's weight of evil will see it.
look.cite: Qur'an 99:6–8 (Az-Zalzalah), paraphrased from Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: The verse chooses the smallest weight its hearers could picture. What claim about judgment does that choice make? How might this passage sound to a poor listener in Mecca and to a rich one?

check.q: What does Qur'an 21:47 say about the scales on the Last Day?
choices: The scales weigh gold, not deeds
No one is wronged by even a mustard seed's weight
The scales are kept in the Kaaba
check.why: 21:47 describes scales set up so that no one is wronged by even a mustard seed's weight; the picture is of complete fairness.

check.q: Why did the theme of judgment carry a moral edge in Mecca, according to Muslim readers?
choices: Because it meant the rich who ignored the orphan would answer for it
Because only Meccans would be judged
check.why: The earliest surahs join the Last Day to justice for the poor, so those who cheated or ignored orphans would answer.

check.q: Which statement about the Day of Judgment is correct?
choices: Muslims across all schools believe in it, but differ on details like the scales
Only Shia Muslims believe in it
It is found only in the Medinan surahs
check.why: Belief in the Day of Judgment is shared across Islam as an article of faith, while readers differ on whether the scales are literal.

lessons.title: Gardens and Fire
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an describes paradise as gardens with rivers and hell as fire, and Muslim readers have taken these pictures both literally and as images.
reading: The Qur'an describes two outcomes after judgment. The first is *Jannah*, "the Garden," the Qur'an's usual word for paradise. It is pictured as gardens beneath which rivers flow, a phrase that appears dozens of times. There are shade, fruit, couches, fine clothing, drink that does not cloud the mind, and companions. Surah 55 lists these gifts with a refrain, and Surah 56 divides those who enter into ranks. Verse 9:72 says the greatest gift there is God's good pleasure.

The second is *Jahannam*, hell, pictured as fire. It has gates, according to 15:44, and guards. The Qur'an describes boiling water, chains and smoke. Verse 4:56 speaks of skins renewed so that the punishment continues. The Qur'an says in 11:106–108 that people stay in fire or garden as long as the heavens and earth last, "except as thy Lord willeth," a phrase scholars have long discussed.

How to read these pictures has divided Muslim scholars. Most classical commentators, such as Ibn Kathir, read them as real descriptions of real places. Some philosophers, such as Ibn Sina (Avicenna, d. 1037), read them as images for states of the soul. Al-Ghazali attacked that reading. Sufi poets often wrote that they wanted God, not gardens. Rabi'a of Basra, a woman mystic of the 700s, is remembered for saying she would put out hell and burn paradise so that people would love God for God alone.

Two more debates matter. First, whether hell is forever. Ibn Taymiyya and his student Ibn al-Qayyim, in the 1300s, argued from the phrase "except as thy Lord willeth" that it might end. Most scholars disagreed. Second, who enters the Garden. Verse 2:62 names Jews, Christians and Sabians who believe in God and the Last Day and do right. Muslim commentators read that verse in different ways, some broadly and some narrowly. The course records the range.

words.d: "the Garden," the Qur'an's usual word for paradise, pictured with rivers, shade and fruit
hell in the Qur'an, pictured as fire with gates and guards
a Sufi woman of the 700s remembered for saying she loved God for God alone, not for paradise or fear of hell

look.title: Two Readers of the Garden
look.text: Reader one, a classical commentator: the gardens, rivers and fruit are real, and God can make them as described. Reader two, a Sufi poet: the true reward is God's presence, and a lover of God does not think about gardens. Both readers cite Qur'an 9:72, which lists gardens and rivers and then says the greatest thing is God's good pleasure.
look.prompt: How can both readers use the same verse? Does 9:72 support one reading more than the other, or does it hold both? Explain with the verse's order of ideas.

check.q: What phrase does the Qur'an use dozens of times for paradise?
check.why: "Gardens beneath which rivers flow" is the Qur'an's most repeated picture of Jannah.

check.q: How did Ibn Sina (Avicenna) read the Qur'an's pictures of paradise and hell?
choices: As descriptions of Mecca and Medina
As real places in every detail
As images for states of the soul
check.why: Ibn Sina read the pictures as images of the soul's states, a view al-Ghazali attacked and most commentators rejected.

check.q: What did Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn al-Qayyim argue about hell?
choices: That it is in the Kaaba
That it might not last forever, based on "except as thy Lord willeth"
check.why: They read 11:106–108's "except as thy Lord willeth" to mean hell might end; most scholars disagreed.

lessons.title: Mercy Above All
lessons.mainIdea: Mercy is the attribute of God the Qur'an repeats most, and Muslim readers hold that it frames every other theme, including judgment.
reading: Count the names of God in the Qur'an, and the names of mercy win. Ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim open every surah but one. Al-Ghafur, the Forgiving, and at-Tawwab, the One who turns back to people, appear dozens of times. Verse 6:12 says God has written mercy upon Himself. Verse 7:156 has God say that His mercy embraces all things. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim reports that God's mercy outweighs God's anger.

For Muslim readers, this frames the Last Day. Judgment is pictured as fair, but mercy comes first. The Qur'an repeats that God accepts *tawba*, repentance, from anyone who turns back. Verse 39:53 tells those who have gone too far against themselves not to despair, because God forgives all sins. Commentators call this one of the most hopeful verses in the book. Surah 93, Ad-Duha, comforts Muhammad himself, and ends by telling him not to turn away the orphan or the beggar.

Mercy is also a duty for people. The Qur'an tells believers to be merciful to parents, to free captives, to feed the poor, and to forgive. Verse 21:107 calls Muhammad a mercy to all the worlds, and Muslim teachers use that verse to say that his followers must show mercy too. The Sufi tradition made divine mercy its center. The jurists made it a rule of reading: when a text is unclear, choose the reading that eases rather than burdens.

Historians of religion note that mercy and judgment stand together in the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament as well. Exodus 34:6 calls God merciful and gracious. The Qur'an, addressed to hearers who knew such language, made mercy the first word of every chapter. How to balance mercy and judgment is a question every one of the three traditions has asked. Each answers it from its own book.

words.d: repentance, turning back to God; the Qur'an says God accepts it from anyone who sincerely turns
a name of God meaning the One who turns back toward people, accepting their repentance
Surah 93, The Morning Hours, a Meccan surah of comfort that ends by protecting the orphan and beggar

look.title: Mercy Written Down
look.text: In Surah 6, God is described as having written mercy upon Himself. In Surah 7, God says His punishment reaches whom He wills, but His mercy embraces all things. In Surah 39, those who have gone too far against themselves are told not to despair of God's mercy, since God forgives all sins.
look.cite: Qur'an 6:12, 7:156 and 39:53, paraphrased from Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Put the three verses next to the pictures of judgment and fire from the last two lessons. How do Muslim readers hold both sets of verses at once? What does "written upon Himself" claim?

check.q: Which attribute of God does the Qur'an repeat most, according to this lesson?
check.why: The names of mercy, ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim, open every surah but one, and mercy is the most repeated attribute.

check.q: What does tawba mean?
check.why: Tawba is repentance; the Qur'an says God accepts it, and at-Tawwab is God's name as the One who turns back to people.

check.q: What rule of reading did Muslim jurists draw from the theme of mercy?
choices: When a text is unclear, choose the reading that eases rather than burdens
Read every verse as a law
check.why: Jurists made a principle of ease from the Qur'an's emphasis on mercy, favoring the lighter reading when a text is unclear.

review.q: What is Surah 112, Al-Ikhlas, mainly about?
review.why: Al-Ikhlas states in four verses that God is one, has no parent or child, and has no equal.

review.q: Every surah but one opens with the basmala, which names God as:
review.why: The basmala reads, in Pickthall, "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful," the two names of mercy.

review.q: The Throne Verse says that no one intercedes with God except:
review.why: 2:255 asks, "Who is he that intercedeth with Him save by His leave?", limiting intercession to God's permission.

review.q: What is the second meaning of the word ayah, besides "verse"?
review.why: Ayah means a verse and also a sign; the Qur'an calls rain, stars and the camel signs that point to God.

review.q: Which of these describes jinn in the Qur'an?
choices: Beings of light who cannot disobey
Beings of smokeless fire who can choose belief or unbelief
The angels who write down deeds
review.why: Qur'an 55:15 says jinn are made of smokeless fire, and Surah 72 shows some believing and some not.

review.q: Which prophet is named most often in the Qur'an, and which earlier book is named most often?
review.why: Musa (Moses) is named well over a hundred times, and the Tawrat, the Torah, is the earlier book named most.

review.q: According to Qur'an 99:7–8, what will each person see on the Last Day?
choices: Even an atom's weight of good or evil they did
review.why: Surah 99 says whoever did an atom's weight of good or evil will see it; the smallest weight stands for complete fairness.

review.q: How did Rabi'a of Basra and other Sufis speak about paradise?
choices: They wanted God for God's sake, not the gardens
They said paradise was in Mecca
They said only Sufis could enter
review.why: Rabi'a is remembered for saying she would burn paradise and put out hell so people would love God alone.
